title: jqBench: a benchmark for reading and editing JSON from natural language and/or examples
claim: Raw community Q&A threads can be automatically extracted and converted into executable, test-verified benchmark tasks through a staged procedure.
layout: 3 stages, left-to-right, arrows between headers, stars mark benchmark components
description: A three-stage left-to-right pipeline titled Conversation → Extract → Convert, with long arrows between the stage headers. On the left is a Stack Overflow screenshot with a question (Q) about converting comma-delimited JSON, and an accepted answer (A) with a jq command, input and output. The middle stage extracts three numbered items: a natural-language instruction, candidate jq programs, and example input/output. The instruction and the examples are shown in gray boxes, and the candidates are in blue monospace. The right stage shows an LLM robot icon prompting an agent with add_test and run_code tools. Double-headed arrows link the tool calls to a test table and to result boxes. Failures appear in red, successes in green, and a red strikethrough marks a wrong value. Black stars mark the components that are part of the benchmark.
caption: Overview of extraction and conversion of Stack Overflow conversations to JQSTACK tasks. Components tagged with a star (⋆) are part of the benchmark.
abstract: We introduce jqBench, a new benchmark for evaluating language models on JSON querying and transformation tasks, where the intent can be given specified using natural language and/or examples. Whereas jqBench is mainly aimed at using the jq tool, it can be used to evaluate other programming languages that query and/or transform JSON. Benchmarks are automatically created from two rich sources of data: Stack Overflow discussions (1496 instances with instructions and examples, called jqStack) and the Spider dataset for SQL generation from natural language (859 instances with instructions and JSON Schema, called jqSpider). We describe and analyze the automated pipeline for benchmark creation, and perform extensive baseline experiments on different models to analyze the complexity and failure modes. Using implicit feedback, the best model (Opus 4.1) scores 76% on the jqStack benchmarks and 81% on the jqSpider benchmarks. Additionally, we show (1) that access to the documentation surprisingly does not help, (2) jq lags behind Python, and (3) that automatic feedback (and therefore examples) is crucial. Besides the challenging benchmarks, we release 13K converted but filtered cases for training purposes.
